His sect was politically influential and enjoyed the patronage and regulation of the shogunate. || The nobility, high-Ranking warriors in Kyoto and Kamakura, and powerful regional lords. |- | {{ill|Sōtō Zen|ja|曹洞宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sōtō Zen|qq=}} || {{ill|Dōgen|ja|道元|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōgen|qq=}}
{{ill|1200|ja|1200年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1200|qq=}}–{{ill|1253|ja|1253rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1253|qq=}} || Emphasizes that solely by “zazen” (shikan taizan – just sitting meditation) one attains enlightenment, with a focus on strict ascetic practices and avoiding engagement with worldly politics. || Mid-Ranking warriors and farmers in the provinces. |} In other words, the Pure Land sects (Pure Land Buddhism, True Pure Land Buddhism, and Jishū) that emphasize reliance on Amitābha’s other-power, the Tendai-based Lotus sect (Nichiren Buddhism), and the Zen sects (Rinzai and Sōtō) which stress self-power through meditation, together represent Kamakura Buddhism. Under the ideology of “protecting the nation” (chin-go kokka), the Nara period’s six Southern Buddhist sects (Nara Buddhism) originally functioned as a scholarly collective,{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.19-47|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} and even in Heian Buddhism, both the exoteric (kenkyō) and the esoteric (mikkyo) schools—though requiring rigorous practice and superhuman abilities—were still essentially Buddhism of the aristocracy. In contrast, these six sects primarily spread among the newly emergent warrior class and the general populace. Even Pure Land teachings, which had flourished during the Kokufu culture of the earlier period (and which during the Heian period were supported by the economic power behind the widespread construction of Amida halls), generally came to be characterized in Kamakura Buddhism by the following features: :* Igyō (ease of practice): not demanding severe asceticism :* Senchaku (selective practice): choosing one method of salvation :* Senjū (devoted practice): single-mindedly committed to that method These characteristics were particularly evident in the Pure Land sects – Pure Land Buddhism, True Pure Land Buddhism, and Jishū – which termed themselves the “Other-Power, Easy Practice school.” Although they criticized Zen (which practices zazen) as a “self-power” method that is overly difficult, in choosing one method and committing wholeheartedly, Zen also shared an element common to other new sects of the Kamakura period. From the twelfth century onward—a period of profound transformation—people, experiencing a series of wars, famines, and the advent of Mappō (the Age of Degenerate Dharma), sought new salvation in Buddhism. In response, Buddhist teachings that emphasized the method of faith and practice—nembutsu and daimoku, as well as Zen teachings—were introduced. These approaches were acceptable not only to the commoners but also to the newly rising warrior class. In permeating deeply into popular life, Kamakura Buddhism (or “Kamakura New Buddhism”) is often seen as a manifestation of the “Japanization” of Buddhism originally transmitted from the continent.{{PDFlink|[http://csc.tsukuba.ac.jp/csc/kenkyu/csc_kenkyu_j_imai_02a.pdf “Japanese Culture and Buddhism – On the Pure Land monk Shinran (1173–1262)”]}}{{ill|Imai Masaharu|ja|今井雅晴|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imai Masaharu|qq=}} (2006) == The Founding of the Pure Land Schools == === Hōnen and Pure Land Buddhism === {{main|Hōnen|Pure Land Buddhism}} {{File:Takanobu-no-miei.jpg|150px|left|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Hōnen|ja|法然|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōnen|qq=}} (Genkū)}} Born in a powerful family of {{ill|Mimasaka Province|1=Mimasaka Province|2=ja|3=美作国|ja|美作国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mimasaka Province|qq=}}, {{ill|Hōnen|ja|法然|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hōnen|qq=}} (1133–1212) entered the Buddhist path at the age of nine after the night attack by warriors on his family – an event following the will of his father, {{ill|Shitsuma Tokikuni|ja|漆間時国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shitsuma Tokikuni|qq=}} (as recorded in his father’s last words) – to dedicate himself to the Buddhist path for the sake of his parents’ repose.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.80-84|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} In {{ill|1147|ja|1147年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1147|qq=}} (the 3rd year of Kyūan), at the ordination platform (kaidan) of Enryaku-ji on {{ill|Mount Hiei|ja|比叡山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Hiei|qq=}} he received precepts from the Tendai head teacher {{ill|Gyōgen|ja|行玄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gyōgen|qq=}}.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.19-47|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Initially, he studied Tendai doctrine under the guidance of the Imperial circle (such as at the inner gate of Mount Hiei) but, dissatisfied with that way of life, he sought not a doctrine of “enlightenment” but one of “salvation.” He transferred to the hermitage of Kurotani Betsusho,Kurotani Betsusho was an organization separate from Enryaku-ji even though it was located on Mount Hiei; it was the dwelling place of a holy man who had left the official priesthood. It can be seen as a borderline space between state temples and the secular world. (松尾（1995）p.30) where he studied Pure Land teachings under the renowned scholar {{ill|Eikū|ja|叡空|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eikū|qq=}} – adopting the name “Hōnen Bō Genkū”.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）pp.68-70|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}}[https://1000ya.isis.ne.jp/1239.html {{ill|Matsuoka Masakō's Thousand Nights, Thousand Volumes: Selected Teachings on Nembutsu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuoka Masakō's Thousand Nights, Thousand Volumes: Selected Teachings on Nembutsu|qq=}}] His extensive reading of all the sutras (five complete readings) earned him the epithet “Hōnen Bō, the First of Wisdom”.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.94-96|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} Both his teacher Eikū and his master’s teacher {{ill|Ryōnin|ja|良忍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryōnin|qq=}} (founder of the Yūzū Nembutsu school) were devoted to the Pure Land teachings found in {{ill|Gen-shin|ja|源信|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gen-shin|qq=}}’s “Outline of Rebirth.” However, their practice recognized other practices besides nembutsu as valid methods for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. In {{ill|1175|ja|1175年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1175|qq=}} (the 5th year of Shōan), Hōnen – then still a student at Kurotani Betsusho – began preaching the doctrine of “exclusive recitation of the nembutsu” (senjū nembutsu), asserting that if one sincerely recites “Namu Amida Butsu” in full trust in the vows of Amitābha Buddha, then rebirth in the Pure Land is assured, basing his teachings on the commentary on the Infinite Life Sutra by the Tang dynasty monk {{ill|Shandō|ja|善導|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shandō|qq=}}.Some scholars date Hōnen’s conversion (the return to Pure Land teachings) later – for example, Inoue Kōte, Akamatsu Toshihide, and Fukui Yasuhiro have proposed dates ranging from 1190 to 1204. Amitābha’s vows (the original vow of Amida) refer to the 48 vows he made when he was still a practitioner known as “Hōzō Bhikṣu,” and his promise to save all beings provided all these vows were fulfilled. Since Hōzō Bhikṣu had already attained Buddhahood ten aeons ago, it would seem that all the vows had been fulfilled.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.137-140|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} Hōnen rejected all the arduous practices of the exoteric and esoteric paths as “difficult” and “extravagant” and insisted that reciting the nembutsu was the only proper practice. In {{ill|1186|ja|1186年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1186|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Bunji), at the Jōrokudō of the Daidō-in of Ōhara, more than twenty scholar-monks – including representatives from Enryaku-ji (Eiben, Chikai, and Shōshin), the Sanron school (Myōben), the Hossō school (Jōkei), the nembutsu sect of Saga’s Ōmiya-in (Nembutsu-bō), and nembutsu monk {{ill|Chōgen|ja|重源|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōgen|qq=}} – as well as over 300 lay listeners, gathered for a great Ōhara debate in which Hōnen expounded his true meaning.{{ill|Seigōhounen|ja|松岡正剛の千夜千冊『正法眼蔵』|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seigōhounen|qq=}} Here, Hōnen described himself as “an ordinary, unthinking person” and argued fervently that one should devote oneself not to the mere contemplation (kannen, imagining the Buddha or Pure Land in one’s mind) or the mere observation of the Buddha (kanbutsu) but to the recitation of the nembutsu. This moment marked a historical turning point that signaled the beginning of the reform movement later known as “Kamakura Buddhism.” Based in Higashiyama’s Yoshimizu, Hōnen’s teaching of nembutsu spread not only among the central nobles – such as Kujō Kanemitsu and other officials anxious about the dawn of a new era – but also among senior warriors like {{ill|Hei Shigehira|ja|平重衡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hei Shigehira|qq=}} as well as ordinary warriors and commoners. In {{ill|1189|ja|1189年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1189|qq=}} (the 5th year of Bunji), he even received ordination from Kanemitsu, and in {{ill|1190|ja|1190年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1190|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kenkyū) he lectured on the three Pure Land sutras at Tōdai-ji at the request of the nembutsu preacher {{ill|Chōgen|ja|重源|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōgen|qq=}}. In response to Kanemitsu’s request, a work recording his doctrines – the “Selected Collected Teachings on Nembutsu” – was composed, believed to have been completed around {{ill|1198|ja|1198年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1198|qq=}} (the 9th year of Kenkyū).In works such as “Hōnen Jōnin Gyōjō Eizzu”, it is suggested that the actual writing was undertaken by disciples such as Anraku-bō Sonsei and Shinkan-bō Kansai. Moreover, Hōnen’s teachings spread not only in Kyoto but also among warriors and farmers of the eastern provinces such as {{ill|Kumagaya Naomichi|ja|熊谷直実|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kumagaya Naomichi|qq=}}, {{ill|Utsunomiya Yoritsuna|ja|宇都宮頼綱|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Utsunomiya Yoritsuna|qq=}}, and {{ill|Yūki Asakō|ja|結城朝光|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūki Asakō|qq=}}.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} In an era marked by constant warfare and a life-and-death struggle, Hōnen’s teaching offered not only new hope for salvation to the warriors but also provided a means to counter the established authorities – such as the temple complexes of the Tendai and Shingon schools that controlled the manors – by advocating a monotheistic faith in Amitābha alone.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Notably, Hōnen was the first in Japanese Buddhist history to widely propagate his teachings among laywomen; he severed his ties with state power and demonstrated his commitment to individual salvation.{{ill|Ienaga (1982)|ja|家永（1982）pp.128-129|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ienaga (1982)|qq=}} However, his exclusive recitation teaching encountered vehement opposition from the established Buddhist community. For instance, the Tendai head priest {{ill|Jien|ja|慈円|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jien|qq=}} criticized Hōnen for asserting that one should recite only the nembutsu and refrain from other practices, denouncing it as the “foolish practice of an odd female ascetic” and claiming that nembutsu was embraced by the unlearned and ignorant.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} In {{ill|1204|ja|1204年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1204|qq=}} (the 1st year of Genkyū), in order to avoid state persecution, Hōnen proposed a seven-article code of precepts to his disciples, seeking their consent. Nevertheless, he was criticized by {{ill|Jōkei|ja|貞慶|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkei|qq=}} of the Hossō school (Hōnen’s critics) and was further denounced by the masses of both the southern and northern Buddhist traditions. In {{ill|1207|ja|1207年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1207|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Ken'ei/ Shōgen), he faced severe state repression (known as the “Ken'ei Persecution”).{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} Even while journeying to his place of exile, Hōnen continued his proselytizing; though he settled temporarily on {{ill|Shioabu Island|ja|塩飽島|lt=Shioabu Island|lt_ja=塩飽島|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shioabu Island|qq=}} (in Sanuki Province), he was pardoned after about ten months.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} For several subsequent years he remained in {{ill|Settsu Province|ja|摂津国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Settsu Province|qq=}}, and in {{ill|1211|ja|1211年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1211|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kenryaku) he returned to Kyoto, moving to Higashiyama Ōtani; however, the following year he passed away there.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Incidentally, after Hōnen’s death, the monk {{ill|Myōe|ja|明恵|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōe|qq=}} of the Kegon school wrote a critique of the “Selected Collected Teachings on Nembutsu” titled {{ill|Sai gyarin|ja|摧邪輪|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sai gyarin|qq=}}. {{File:Main Hall, Chion-in - IMG 5082.JPG|300px|right|thumb|The Go-kage-dō of {{ill|Chion-in|ja|知恩院|lt=Chion-in|lt_ja=知恩院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chion-in|qq=}} (a National Treasure)}} The rapid spread of Pure Land Buddhism was partly due to the simplicity of its practice – salvation by performing meritorious acts through the recitation of the nembutsu – but it also owed much to its musical and performative character (the nembutsu was at times known as “nōshō”, linking it to the performing arts).{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}}In Torakane Shiren’s “Genkō Shakusho”, the terms “nōdoku,” “nōshō,” and “nōsetsu” are collectively described as “ongei” (performing arts). Moreover, Hōnen’s exclusive nembutsu teaching sparked debates about whether reciting the nembutsu many times (ta-nengi) or only once (ichinengi) was the proper method; although Hōnen himself acknowledged the “one-shot” position, he personally practiced with a “many-shot” approach. His disciple {{ill|Shinran|ja|親鸞|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinran|qq=}} later adopted the “one-shot” stance.{{ill|Ishii (1974)|ja|石井（1974）pp.429-430|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishii (1974)|qq=}} From among Hōnen’s many disciples who helped spread Pure Land Buddhism, one notable figure was {{ill|Bennchō|ja|弁長|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bennchō|qq=}}, a man born into a warrior family in {{ill|Chikushi Province|ja|筑前国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chikushi Province|qq=}}. Bennchō went to Kyoto and became one of Hōnen’s disciples; he then spread the teachings in {{ill|Chikugo Province|ja|筑後国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chikugo Province|qq=}} from his base at {{ill|Zendō-ji|ja|善導寺|lt=Zendō-ji|lt_ja=善導寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zendō-ji|qq=}}, establishing what became known as the {{ill|Chinzei-ha|ja|鎮西派|lt=Chinzei faction|lt_ja=鎮西派|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinzei-ha|qq=}} and later extending his efforts into the Kantō region through his disciple {{ill|Ryōchū|ja|良忠|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryōchū|qq=}}, a native of {{ill|Iwami Province|ja|石見国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwami Province|qq=}}.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）pp.70-72|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} Additionally, a Kyoto-born disciple named {{ill|Shōkū|ja|証空|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōkū|qq=}} later founded the “Nishiyama-ha” at {{ill|Zenpō-ji|ja|善峯寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenpō-ji|qq=}} on the western slopes of Kyoto. {{see|Karyoku no Hōnan (The Persecution of Hōnen)}} Thus, while Pure Land Buddhism spread nationwide, it was again suppressed in {{ill|1227|ja|1227年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1227|qq=}} (the 3rd year of {{ill|Karoku|ja|嘉禄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Karoku|qq=}}). There was even an incident in which Hōnen’s tomb was desecrated by monk-soldiers from Mount Hiei, yet his teachings continued to gain traction even within the imperial court.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} His disciple {{ill|Genshi|ja|源智|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Genshi|qq=}} later enshrined Hōnen’s remains at Ōtani, and based on the annual knowledge ceremonies held on his memorial day ({{ill|Gekkō-nichi|ja|月命日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gekkō-nichi|qq=}}), founded the head temple of Pure Land Buddhism, {{ill|Chion-in|ja|知恩院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chion-in|qq=}}.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} === Shinran and True Pure Land Buddhism === {{main|Shinran|True Pure Land Buddhism}} {{File:ShinranShonin.png|150px|left|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Shinran|ja|親鸞|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinran|qq=}}}} Believed to be of the Hino family, {{ill|Shinran|ja|親鸞|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinran|qq=}} (1173–1262) ascended Mount Hiei at the age of nine and was given the name “Han’en”.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.84-89|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} He spent nearly twenty years studying at Enryaku-ji but could not attain enlightenment, and in {{ill|1201|ja|1201st year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1201|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kennin) he took up residence at {{ill|Chōdō-ji (Rokkakudō)|ja|六角堂|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōdō-ji (Rokkakudō)|qq=}} in Kyoto—a temple popularly venerated by the common people—where, reportedly guided by a dream of {{ill|Shōtoku Taishi|ja|聖徳太子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōtoku Taishi|qq=}}, he sought Hōnen’s door.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} It is said that Shinran was so deeply devoted to his master Hōnen that he vowed, “Even if deceived by the Venerable Hōnen and destined for hell by the nembutsu, I shall never regret it.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} During the {{ill|1207|ja|1207年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1207|qq=}} persecution (the “Ken'ei Persecution”), Shinran was deprived of his monastic status and exiled to {{ill|Echigo Province|ja|越後国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Echigo Province|qq=}}. He was pardoned four years later. Already practicing the renunciation of marriage and consumption of meat, Shinran, upon hearing of Hōnen’s death, remained in Echigo. In {{ill|1214|ja|1214年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1214|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Kenpō), at the age of 42, accompanied by his wife {{ill|Keishin-ni|ja|恵信尼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishin-ni|qq=}} and his children, he set out on a missionary journey to the eastern provinces and established a small hermitage known as the “Grass Hut of Inada” in {{ill|Hitachi Province|ja|常陸国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hitachi Province|qq=}}.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Shinran inherited, developed, and deepened his master Hōnen’s teachings,{{ill|Honda (S.K.S.)|ja|本多弘之『新講 教行信証』総序の巻、P.46。|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honda (S.K.S.)|qq=}} and began writing his seminal work, the “Kyōgyō Shinjō”, at Inada. He preached absolute reliance on other-power (zettai tariki): that mere faith in Amitābha Buddha (shinjin-i hon) was sufficient for rebirth (ketsujō) in the Pure Land; furthermore, he argued that those who were deeply conscious of their sinful nature (the “evil persons”) were precisely those whom the Buddha intended to save (the “evil person, correct mechanism” doctrine).{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} Shinran’s uncompromising stance on absolute other-power is exemplified by his teaching on the “power of the vow” – where the faithful not only recite the nembutsu as a practice but are also, according to Shinran, preordained by Amitābha Buddha’s vow (via kaikyō) to be reborn in the Pure Land regardless of any personal merit.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.96-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} Thus, the nembutsu recited here is not an “action” nor a meritorious deed but rather a grateful act of repayment (hōon nembutsu).{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.96-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} This concept is akin in some respects to the Tendai notion of “hon-bokaku” (original enlightenment).{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.96-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} The famous passage from Shinran’s disciple {{ill|Yui-en|ja|唯円|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yui-en|qq=}}’s work, “Even the virtuous attain rebirth, let alone the wicked,” is widely quoted. This originated from Shinran’s own self-reflection—realizing that he himself was too sinful to even possess the pure mind depicted in the eighteenth vow.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.96-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} Shinran argued that if those capable of self-powered meritorious actions (“the virtuous”) could be saved, then how much more could those burdened by sin (“the wicked”) be saved by virtue of harboring within them the very cause of Amitābha’s vow.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.137-140|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} Moreover, in front of Amitābha Buddha, everyone is equal; there are no masters or disciples – all are fellow practitioners.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} It is also pointed out that Shinran’s deepening of his thought is closely related to the harrowing spectacle of the Great Famine of {{ill|Kan’ki|ja|寛喜の大飢饉|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kan’ki|qq=}} (1230–1231) that he witnessed in Hitachi Province.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.137-140|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} As for his commentary on the “Tannishō,” in the Muromachi period the monk {{ill|Rennyo|ja|蓮如|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rennyo|qq=}} – who devoted himself to spreading True Pure Land Buddhism (Jōdo Shinshū) – wrote a preface stating that the Tannishō should not be given indiscriminately to those lacking the “good roots” of one’s past life.{{ill|Seigō Shinran|ja|松岡正剛の千夜千冊『歎異抄』|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seigō Shinran|qq=}} After {{ill|1231|ja|1231st year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1231|qq=}} (the 3rd year of {{ill|Kankei|ja|寛喜|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kankei|qq=}}), Shinran returned to Kyoto accompanied by his youngest daughter {{ill|Kakushin-ni|ja|覚信尼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kakushin-ni|qq=}}. Though he lived in poverty after his return, Shinran taught that those who had attained rebirth in the Pure Land would reappear in the world to rescue others through a process of re-incarnation (kansō kaikyō), completed his “Kyōgyō Shinjō,” and composed hymns (wasan) for his fellow practitioners in the eastern provinces.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Later, in {{ill|1256|ja|1256年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1256|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kōgen), while in the eastern provinces, he broke with his eldest son {{ill|Zenran|ja|善鸞|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenran|qq=}}—who had introduced magical elements into nembutsu practice—and in his final years renounced all self-reliance, entrusting himself entirely to the power of {{ill|Amitābha Buddha|ja|阿弥陀仏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amitābha Buddha|qq=}} in what is regarded as a state of natural law (jinen hōni). Shinran, who died at the age of 90, later reflected on his life as one steeped in sin and even left instructions to have his body cremated and his ashes cast into the Kamo River.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Beyond any salvific magic, Shinran’s teaching – which preached a purified faith in the next life – eventually formed the basis of what came to be known as {{ill|Jōdo Shinshū|ja|浄土真宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōdo Shinshū|qq=}}; in {{ill|1272|ja|1272nd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1272|qq=}} (the 9th year of Bun'ei) the great memorial hall of Ōtani was built.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.137-140|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} The memorial hall was constructed on land formerly owned by {{ill|Onomiya Zen'nenn|ja|小野宮禅念|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Onomiya Zen'nenn|qq=}}, the second husband of Kakushin-ni, and in {{ill|1321|ja|1321st year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1321|qq=}} (the 1st year of Genkō) it was renamed Ōtani Hongan-ji. The name “Hongan-ji” was sanctioned by directives from {{ill|Mori Kuninori Prince|ja|守邦親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Kuninori Prince|qq=}} in {{ill|1332|ja|1332nd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1332|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Genkō) and from {{ill|Goryō Prince|ja|護良親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Goryō Prince|qq=}}, a son of Emperor Go-Daigo, the following year.{{ill|Kuroda (1979)|ja|黒田（1979）pp.221-253|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuroda (1979)|qq=}} === The Ken'ei Persecution and Religious Freedom === {{main|Ken'ei Persecution}} In {{ill|1207|ja|1207年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1207|qq=}}, Hōnen’s Yoshimizu sect was denounced by Enryaku-ji and Kōfuku-ji. Under orders from the retired Emperor {{ill|Go-Toba|ja|後鳥羽上皇|lt=Emperor Go-Toba|lt_ja=後鳥羽上皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go-Toba|qq=}}, the exclusive nembutsu practice was suspended, and among Hōnen’s disciples, four—including Anraku-bō {{ill|Sonsei|ja|遵西|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sonsei|qq=}} and {{ill|Jūren|ja|住蓮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jūren|qq=}}—were sentenced to death; furthermore, Hōnen himself along with seven leading disciples including Shinran were exiled. Hōnen, who at the age of 75 was stripped of his monk status and given the secular name “Fujiwara Motohiko,” is said to have remarked, “Even if the death penalty is imposed, the nembutsu shall never be halted. To be able to preach the nembutsu even among the rustic peasants in remote lands is, if anything, an expression of filial piety toward the Imperial grace.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Shinran, then 34, parted ways with his aged master and, exiled under the secular name “Fujiwara Zenshin,” came to be known in Echigo as “Gutoku” or simply “Toku,” steadfastly defining his life as one outside both the monkhood and the laity.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Here, Shinran not only asserted “freedom of religion” to the Imperial Court but also voiced his protest against the state repression—a moment regarded as revolutionary in the history of Japanese thought.{{ill|Ienaga (1982)|ja|家永（1982）pp.128-129|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ienaga (1982)|qq=}} === Ippen and the Jishū === {{main|Ippen|Jishū}} {{File:IPPEN.JPG|200px|left|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Ippen|ja|一遍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ippen|qq=}}}} In the mid-Kamakura period, the itinerant monk {{ill|Ippen|ja|一遍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ippen|qq=}} (1239–1289), known as the “Itinerant Ascetic,” is said to have been born into the powerful {{ill|Kii Province|ja|伊予国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kii Province|qq=}}’s {{ill|Kōno clan|ja|河野氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōno clan|qq=}}.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.89-91|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}Currently, a monument titled “Site of the Birth of Ippen” stands at the gate of Hōgen-ji (in Matsuyama, Ehime Prefecture) in Dōgo. Losing his mother at the age of 10, he was ordained in {{ill|1250|ja|1250年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1250|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Kenchō) at the hermitage of the Pure Land sect’s Nishiyama-ha under the monk {{ill|Seitaku|ja|聖達|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seitaku|qq=}} near Dazaifu.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Through Seitaku’s introduction, he studied Pure Land doctrine under a prominent monk named Kādai – to whom he was given the name Chishin – residing in {{ill|Hizen Province|ja|肥前国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hizen Province|qq=}} in Shimizu, and later once again renounced his monkhood in 1263 (taking a wife) to lead a secular life devoted to the Buddha. However, after becoming embroiled in local disputes over estates, he resolved to renounce the karmic cycle of reincarnation and re-ordained, making a pilgrimage to {{ill|Shzenō-ji|ja|善光寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shzenō-ji|qq=}} in {{ill|Shinano Province|ja|信濃国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinano Province|qq=}}.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Subsequently, he returned to his native province of Iyo, engaged in rigorous practice, and then led an itinerant lifestyle, visiting sacred sites across western Japan.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Around {{ill|1274|ja|1274年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1274|qq=}} (the 11th year of Bun'ei), while on a 100‐day pilgrimage through Kumano – after traversing Mount Kōya – Chishin reportedly received a divine oracle from the Kumano deity {{ill|Gongen|ja|熊野権現|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gongen|qq=}} on the day of his full completion. The oracle was composed of four verses whose initial characters of each phrase together form “600,000 people,” and thus the verses are known as the “600,000-People Verse.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Inspired further by this oracle to deepen his nembutsu faith, Chishin began referring to himself as “Ippen” and regarded the itinerant monk {{ill|Kūya|ja|空也|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kūya|qq=}} as his predecessor, inheriting the ancient tradition of nembutsu saints. For the next 15 years he toured extensively from the north in {{ill|Mutsu Province|1=Mutsu Province|2=ja|3=陸奥国|ja|陸奥国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mutsu Province|qq=}} (from Esashi) to the south in {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|薩摩国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|qq=}} and {{ill|Ōsumi Province|ja|大隅国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōsumi Province|qq=}}. In the Jishū, everyday life is viewed as the “time of the dying” – meaning that each day is to be regarded as one’s final moment – and thus one should recite the nembutsu. Ippen distributed paper talismans inscribed with the phrase “{{ill|Namu Amida Butsu, Certain Rebirth for 600,000 People|ja|南無阿弥陀仏、決定往生六十万人|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Namu Amida Butsu, Certain Rebirth for 600,000 People|qq=}}” and recorded the names of those who came to embrace the faith in a register called the “Kanjinchō.” This practice (fusan) eventually came to mean that anyone whose name was recorded was assured of salvation. Over time, this teaching – which did not differentiate on the basis of social status, gender, or even the presence of faith – became established, and from {{ill|1279|ja|1279年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1279|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Kōan) onward, the joy and gratitude of believers were expressed through nembutsu, with recitations sometimes accompanied by a dance known as “Odori Nembutsu.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Ippen is recorded to have stated in his “Collected Sayings of Ippen” that “since both the Buddha and I are essentially one, if one recites ‘Namu Amida Butsu,’ neither the Buddha nor I truly exist,” thereby reflecting the deep interconnection between his Pure Land faith and the Tendai concept of original enlightenment.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.99-100|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} After Ippen’s death, another teacher – {{ill|Tara Amida Butsu|ja|他阿弥陀仏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tara Amida Butsu|qq=}} (of the Shin sect) – emerged, gathering itinerant monks while continuing Ippen’s circuit of pilgrimages. Subsequently, within the Jishū, several branches emerged (later known as the 12 sects of Jishū, including the direct line of the itinerant monks, the Okutani, Rokujō, Shijō, and Ikō groups, among others), often accompanied by internal conflicts and tensions as the Jishū organization solidified.The itinerant group later came to be known as the “Jishū 12 sects.” (Kuroda (1979) p.226) The head temple of the Jishū was established in {{ill|1325|ja|1325年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1325|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Shōchū) at {{ill|Seijō-kōji|ja|清浄光寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seijō-kōji|qq=}} in Fujisawa, Kanagawa Prefecture, founded by the itinerant monk {{ill|Kita Hōjō Tsugitoki|ja|北条貞時|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kita Hōjō Tsugitoki|qq=}}. == The Spread of the Lotus Sect == === Nichiren and the Lotus Sect === {{main|Nichiren|Nichiren Buddhism}} {{File:Nichiren_Daishonin_Hakii_Portrait.jpg|130px|left|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Nichiren|ja|日蓮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren|qq=}}}} At roughly the same time as Ippen’s activities, another reformer emerged based on an ancient Lotus Sutra faith – that of {{ill|Nichiren|ja|日蓮|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren|qq=}} (1222–1282). Born in {{ill|Awa Province|ja|安房国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Awa Province|qq=}}’s {{ill|Chōsa District|ja|長狭郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōsa District|qq=}} in Tōjō, he later described his origins as “the child of a Sennadara” and “the child of a lowly commoner born from a stone in the sea.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.98-101|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}“Sennadara” is the Sino-Japanese reading of the term referring to the lowest of the four varnas in India – even below the outcast Chandalas. Murakami Shigeyoshi (1981) p.98 discusses that this indicates Nichiren’s origin as likely being from the servant class of temple retainers; other scholars such as Irumatase Noriou, Otō Masahide, and Matsuo Takeshi have proposed that he was born into a minor aristocratic family, a commoner, or even the child of a fisherman respectively. Initially, Nichiren entered the Tendai school at {{ill|Seisō-ji (Kamogawa)|ja|清澄寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seisō-ji (Kamogawa)|qq=}} in Kamogawa, Chiba Prefecture, as a young novice, and at the age of 16 took ordination under the name “Renchō.”{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Ambitious to become “the wisest man in Japan,” Nichiren first studied in Kamakura and later traveled extensively through Kyoto, Mount Hiei, and the southern capitals to learn not only Tendai doctrine but also esoteric teachings, Pure Land Buddhism, and Zen. Since at that time Tendai monks (except those associated with {{ill|Enryaku-ji's|ja|園城寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enryaku-ji's|qq=}}) received ordination at Enryaku-ji’s kaidan, it is presumed that Nichiren was ordained there as well.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Amidst the flourishing of Pure Land Buddhism, Mount Hiei was known for its vigorous promotion of the philosophical and mystical Tendai notion of original enlightenment, and using that doctrine it repeatedly suppressed the rising Buddhist movements such as nembutsu; Nichiren, however, rejected any compromise with the Pure Land movement emerging within Tendai and, by advocating a new Lotus Sutra faith, resolved to revive Tendai teaching in the degenerate age.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Nichiren selected the Lotus Sutra (Myōhō Renge Kyō) as the sole authentic teaching of the Buddha and emphasized chanting the daimoku “{{ill|Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|ja|南無妙法蓮華経|lt=Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|lt_ja=南無妙法蓮華経|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|qq=}}” (a practice known as shōdai) as an expression of faith. The phrase “Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō” means “to take refuge in the Lotus Sutra,” and its origin is tied to the title of the scripture.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} In {{ill|1253|ja|1253rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1253|qq=}} (the 5th year of Kenchō), Nichiren returned to Awa and, in the forest of Asahi on Mount Seishō, declared the establishment of his new teaching by chanting the daimoku 10 times.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} The following year he moved to Kamakura and established a hermitage in the area of {{ill|Nagoe|ja|名越|lt=Nagoe|lt_ja=名越|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nagoe|qq=}}. At that time, Kamakura was beset by successive disasters – fires, floods, earthquakes, and recurrent epidemics – and in {{ill|1259|ja|1259年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1259|qq=}} (the 1st year of Shōgen) a widespread famine struck the nation.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Nichiren interpreted these natural calamities as signs of the coming degenerate age (Mappō), attributing them to the abandonment of the true Lotus Sutra by the “heretical” Pure Land sect. In {{ill|1260|ja|1260年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1260|qq=}} (the 1st year of Bun'ō), he wrote the “Risshō Ankoku Ron” – a treatise urging the shogunate (specifically the close aide of the regent {{ill|Hojo Tokiyori|ja|北条時頼|lt=Hojo Tokiyori|lt_ja=北条時頼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hojo Tokiyori|qq=}}) to govern based on the Lotus Sutra. In it he warned that if the “heretical sects” were allowed to continue, then among the seven disasters foretold in the scripture, the “rebellion within one’s own country” and the “invasion from abroad” would inevitably occur.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.106-110|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} Nichiren and his followers looked to the shogunate with hope and publicly debated Buddhist doctrines, but his actions provoked the wrath of nembutsu adherents and his hermitage was torched during the {{ill|Matsubagaya Persecution|ja|松葉ヶ谷法難|lt=Matsubagaya Persecution|lt_ja=松葉ヶ谷法難|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsubagaya Persecution|qq=}}. This persecution occurred roughly one month after he submitted the “Risshō Ankoku Ron” to Tokiyori, and it is believed that powerful figures in the shogunate and allied Buddhist priests were behind the assault – making it one of the most severe instances of state-sponsored persecution in the history of Japan.There is a later legend concerning an attempted secret assassination of Nichiren at Ryūnokuchi in 1271 (the 8th year of Bun'ei) which is now generally regarded as a later fabrication. (Murakami (1981) p.101) After this, Nichiren temporarily took refuge in {{ill|Shimōsa Province|ja|下総国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shimōsa Province|qq=}}, but soon returned to Kamakura and was exiled for over two years to {{ill|Izu Province|ja|伊豆国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Izu Province|qq=}} by the shogunate. Upon being pardoned and returning to his hometown, Nichiren resumed his activities in Kamakura. Unyielding to authority, he vigorously propagated Lotus Sutra faith through public debates (jissen) and challenged rival sects by sharply attacking them with his “Four Pithy Sayings” – “nembutsu unceasing, Zen as the demon of heaven, Shingon as the religion of a fallen state, and precepts as the bandits of the state” – while predicting the imminent arrival of national calamities. His newly established {{ill|Lotus Sect|ja|法華宗|lt=Lotus Sect|lt_ja=法華宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lotus Sect|qq=}} (commonly known as Nichiren Buddhism) soon spread among the warrior class and merchants in the Kantō region; indeed, in {{ill|1268|ja|1268年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1268|qq=}} (the 5th year of Bun'ei) a national edict from the Yuan dynasty arrived at the shogunate, and Nichiren, his prediction about “invasions from abroad” having been vindicated by the edict, urged regent {{ill|Hojo Tokimasa|ja|北条時宗|lt=Hojo Tokimasa|lt_ja=北条時宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hojo Tokimasa|qq=}} to dismiss nembutsu and Zen and to employ him as a “national teacher.” He also exchanged letters with members of other sects – such as those from the Jishū, the courtier {{ill|Hira Reliance|ja|平頼綱|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hira Reliance|qq=}}, {{ill|Rankei Dōryū|ja|蘭渓道隆|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rankei Dōryū|qq=}}, and {{ill|Gonryaku-ji|ja|極楽寺|lt=Gonryaku-ji|lt_ja=極楽寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gonryaku-ji|qq=}}’s disciple {{ill|Ninshō|ja|忍性|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninshō|qq=}} – and challenged them to public doctrinal debates. Nichiren’s teachings, which were steeped in “old Buddhism” elements, also reflected lingering aspects of the national protection ideology (chin-go kokka) prevalent at the time.{{ill|Ienaga (1982)|ja|家永（1982）pp.128-129|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ienaga (1982)|qq=}} {{File:Kuonji-temple-Hondou.jpg|300px|right|thumb|The main hall of {{ill|Kuon-ji|ja|久遠寺|lt=Kuon-ji|lt_ja=久遠寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuon-ji|qq=}}}} In the Lotus Sect, the tradition of revering sutras – through activities such as copying (shakyō), burying, and reciting them from memory – had a long history. This practice was seen not only in the offering of the “Heike Nōkyō” to {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine|ja|厳島神社|lt=Itsukushima Shrine|lt_ja=厳島神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Itsukushima Shrine|qq=}} but also among powerful figures such as the retired Emperor {{ill|Go-Shirakawa|ja|後白河法皇|lt=Go-Shirakawa Hōō|lt_ja=後白河法皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go-Shirakawa|qq=}} – who was known as a “holder of the Lotus Sutra” – and even in the case of {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|ja|源頼朝|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo|lt_ja=源頼朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto no Yoritomo|qq=}}, who was likewise called a “holder of the Lotus Sutra Hachibanzan.”{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）pp.72-74|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} Furthermore, although the Tendai school – founded by {{ill|Saichō|ja|最澄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saichō|qq=}} in the early Heian period – was also known as the “Tendai Lotus Sect” (Tendai Hokke-shū), Nichiren succeeded in establishing his own distinct Lotus Sect (i.e. Nichiren Buddhism) despite inheriting that tradition.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.106-110|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} {{File:Rinmetsudojihonzon.jpg|150px|right|thumb|A mandala representing the ten realms, said to be autographed by Nichiren (housed at {{ill|Myōhon-ji|ja|妙本寺|lt=Myōhon-ji|lt_ja=妙本寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōhon-ji|qq=}} in Kamakura)}} Nichiren’s doctrine held that the Lotus Sutra is the only correct teaching, representing absolute truth transcending both time and space, and that all other doctrines and beliefs are to be rejected.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.101-105|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} The daimoku itself is regarded as embodying truth and is considered a mandala representing the entire universe; Nichiren placed the daimoku centrally and arranged the names of various Buddhas and deities around it in his “Lotus Mandala” – which he enshrined as his principal object of veneration. Furthermore, he established a set of “Five Fundamental Doctrinal Judgments” which declared that in every aspect – teaching, capacity, time, nation, and sequence – the Lotus Sutra was supreme.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.101-105|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Moreover, Nichiren argued that one should rely not on the miraculous power (jumyaku) of the Lotus Sutra but on one’s own self-awakened consciousness as an “actor” (gyō) of its teachings. He also maintained that one must base one’s allegiance not on human power but solely on the Buddha’s truth. He envisioned an ideal in which the laws of the Buddha and those of the state (Ōhō) were united—a “king-Buddha synthesis.” He asserted that unless the state was governed according to the correct Dharma, no proper government could exist, and that even the Emperor, if he strayed from the Dharma, would inevitably incur Buddhist punishment.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.101-105|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Within the “Five Fundamental Doctrinal Judgments,” the emphasis placed on “time” and “nation” has led even to today an unusually active involvement in political issues among the various sects of Nichiren Buddhism.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.101-105|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} == The Spread of Zen and State Patronage by the Shogunate == === The Spread of Zen and the Japanese Daruma Sect === {{main|Japanese Daruma Sect|ja|日本達磨宗}} The teachings of Zen – originating from India through the monk {{ill|Daruma|ja|達磨大師|lt=Daruma|lt_ja=達磨大師|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daruma|qq=}} (Bodhidharma), which emphasize achieving enlightenment through zazen and self-power – had long flourished among the upper echelons of Song China. Zen had already been transmitted to Japan during the Nara period; however, due to its rise in prominence during the Song period, it attracted renewed attention from the late Heian period onward. Although a monk by the name of {{ill|Dainichibō Nōnin|ja|大日房能忍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dainichibō Nōnin|qq=}} (whose dates are uncertain) appeared slightly before Eisai, and established {{ill|Sanbō-ji|ja|三宝寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanbō-ji|qq=}} in Suita in Settsu Province (now part of Osaka Prefecture), thereby being one of the earliest to attempt establishing a Zen institution in Japan, his activities eventually lost their central focus as the Japanese Daruma Sect he founded dissipated during its process of spreading.{{ill|Ishii (1974)|ja|石井（1974）pp.270-271|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishii (1974)|qq=}} However, with the subsequent appearance of figures such as Eisai and Dōgen, Zen spread rapidly. In contrast to the Pure Land school’s emphasis on absolute other-power salvation, Zen’s teaching of attaining rebirth through one’s own self-power resonated with the spirit of the warrior era, which prized self-reliance in problem-solving.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）pp.74-75|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} === Eisai and Rinzai Zen === {{main|Eisai|Rinzai Zen}} {{File:Myoan-Eisai-Kennin-ji-Portrait.png|150px|right|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Eisai|ja|栄西|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisai|qq=}}}} Born into the family of a shrine priest at {{ill|Kibi-tsu Shrine|ja|吉備津神社|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kibi-tsu Shrine|qq=}} in Bitchū, {{ill|Eisai|ja|栄西|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisai|qq=}} (1141–1215) was ordained on Mount Hiei in {{ill|1154|ja|1154年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1154|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kyūju). He then made two trips to Song China. On his first trip, in {{ill|1168|ja|1168年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1168|qq=}} (the 3rd year of Nin'an) he visited Mount Tiantai’s Mannen-ji to study Tendai teachings; however, by that time the temple had already been converted into a Zen institution. Eisai was attracted to Zen and, prompted by the nembutsu monk {{ill|Chōgen|ja|重源|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōgen|qq=}} who was studying in Song, returned to Japan shortly thereafter, dedicating a 60-volume work “Tendai Shōso” to the head of the Tendai school.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.92-95|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} In {{ill|1187|ja|1187年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1187|qq=}} (the 3rd year of Bunji), Eisai again traveled to Song, where over the course of five years he studied Rinzai Zen at temples on Mount Tiantai and Mount Tendō (both in Zhejiang Province, China). Receiving Dharma transmission from Kyokuan Kaishō, he returned to Japan and in {{ill|1191|ja|1191st year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1191|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Kenkyū) established Rinzai Zen.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Initially he devoted himself to propagating Zen in Kyushu – establishing centers in Hakata, Kashii, and Hirado – but eventually returned to Kyoto and advocated that Zen was the correct teaching in the age of Mappō, thereby calling for a Tendai revival through Zen.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} However, on the 5th day of the 7th month of {{ill|1194|ja|1194年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1194|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Kenkyū), an edict to suspend Zen was issued together with that of the Japanese Daruma Sect at Sanbō-ji in Settsu Province, led by figures such as {{ill|Dainichibō Nōnin|ja|大日房能忍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dainichibō Nōnin|qq=}}.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}{{ill|Hanuki (1989)|ja|葉貫（1989）p.419|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanuki (1989)|qq=}} A person by the name of Ryōben from {{ill|Chikushi Province|ja|筑前国|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chikushi Province|qq=}} – not to be confused with the earlier Tendai monk of the same name – complained to the lecture congregation at Enryaku-ji about the increasing number of people entering Zen in Kyushu and even appealed to the Imperial Court to suspend Eisai’s propagation of Zen. In the 6th year of Kenkyū, Kanemitsu (the regent) summoned Eisai to Kyoto and arranged for the white-robed official, {{ill|Shatoni|ja|舎人|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shatoni|qq=}}, to conduct hearings on “What is Zen?” while also having the Great Counselor {{ill|Yomuro Sōrai|ja|葉室宗頼|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yomuro Sōrai|qq=}} attend as an auditor.{{ill|Hanuki (1989)|ja|葉貫（1989）p.419|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hanuki (1989)|qq=}} In response to such pressures, by no later than {{ill|1198|ja|1198年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1198|qq=}} (the 9th year of Kenkyū), Eisai composed the treatise “Kōzen Gokokuron” beginning with “How great is the mind; how profound it is!” In this work he argued that strict precepts form the basis of all Buddhist teaching, that Zen is based on precepts, and that there is no fundamental difference between Zen and the traditional Buddhist doctrines. He further maintained that if one were to elevate precepts above the laws of the state and use Zen to protect the nation, it would be no different from the Tendai teaching pioneered by {{ill|Saichō|ja|最澄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saichō|qq=}}.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）pp.74-75|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}} This work, believed to have been composed in Kyushu, aimed to dispel misconceptions about Zen and clarify its true meaning.[http://www.shofukuji.or.jp/onki/index.htm {{ill|Eisai Zen Master’s 800th Anniversary Memorial Service|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisai Zen Master’s 800th Anniversary Memorial Service|qq=}} (Ankoku-san Seifuku-ji)] Later, at around {{ill|1211|ja|1211年|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1211|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kenryaku), Eisai was appointed as the head of the Zen establishment in Kamakura by the shogunate’s patron, {{ill|Minamoto no Saneshige|ja|源実朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto no Saneshige|qq=}}, and in {{ill|1213|ja|1213rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1213|qq=}} (the 1st year of Kenpō) he even attained the position of “Gon-sōjō” (Head Preceptor) under state patronage. This was extremely rare for a monk who, like Eisai, had once been a “tosses” (脱世僧).{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}According to the work “Sasekijū” (compiled in 1283), all but one of the 46 individuals appointed as Tōdai Daikanjō from 1181 (the 1st year of Yōwa) to 1527 (the 7th year of Daiei) were tosses. (松尾（1995）p.70) {{File:Kenninji Kyoto06n4272.jpg|300px|left|thumb|The Hōdō of {{ill|Kenninji|ja|建仁寺|lt=Kenninji|lt_ja=建仁寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kenninji|qq=}}}} == Dōgen and Sōtō Zen == {{main|Dōgen|Sōtō Zen}} The founder of Sōtō Zen, {{ill|Dōgen|ja|道元|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōgen|qq=}} (1200–1253), was born in Kyoto as the son of {{ill|Tsuchimikado Michichika|ja|土御門通親|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado Michichika|qq=}} (also known as Hisatagō), a former Minister of the Right. (A note: Dōgen’s maternal uncle later became Emperor {{ill|Tsuchimikado Tennō|ja|土御門天皇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchimikado Tennō|qq=}} and was one of the exiled princes implicated in the 【承久の乱】; however, Dōgen himself had no involvement in the rebellion and left for Tosa Province of his own accord.) Dōgen lost both his parents at a young age and entered the Buddhist path early, being ordained at Mount Hiei at the age of 13 to study Tendai doctrine.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.95-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Advised to study Zen in China for a deeper understanding of the Buddha’s teachings, Dōgen studied under {{ill|Myōzen|ja|明全|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōzen|qq=}} at Kenninji – established by Eisai – and in {{ill|1223|ja|1223rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1223|qq=}} (the 2nd year of Jōtō) he traveled to Song China, where he spent nearly five years studying Zen before finally receiving Dharma transmission from the monk {{ill|Nyōjō|ja|天童如浄|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nyōjō|qq=}} on Mount Tendō. With this, he attained the state of enlightenment (“shinkin datsuroku”, literally “the falling away of body and mind”) and received the formal seal of transmission.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.95-98|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.101-106|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} Sōtō Zen is also known as “Mokusho Zen” (silent illumination Zen) and emphasizes that by simply engaging in zazen one can realize the innate nature of the self and attain enlightenment. Dōgen taught the practice of “shikantaza” (just sitting) – a method of zazen in which all discursive thought is abandoned – as the very expression of one’s Buddha nature. Although he also performed ritualized prayers (kaji kitō), these were intended not as meritorious practices but as a means to strip away all superfluous attachments from conventional Buddhism. Consequently, his reform movement – which came to be known as “Sōtō Zen” – was subject to increasing persecution by the monks of Enryaku-ji.{{ill|Seigō Dōgen|ja|松岡正剛の千夜千冊『正法眼蔵』|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seigō Dōgen|qq=}} Dōgen expounded a teaching that rejected reliance on precepts or esoteric rituals, instead emphasizing that through zazen one naturally comes to realize one’s Buddha nature, thereby attaining enlightenment. His doctrine of “shūshō ittō” (practice and realization are one and the same) asserts that there is no end to practice and no beginning to enlightenment – that zazen is not merely a means to attain enlightenment but is itself the act of being a Buddha. In his view, when one sits in zazen in a state of no-mind, one is already the awakened one, and zazen becomes the act of a Buddha. Nevertheless, this does not imply complacency; rather, because one is a Buddha, one must continue endless practice.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.101-106|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} From this, it follows that every aspect of daily life becomes practice. Although Dōgen himself originally did not intend to found a new sect, his disciples who gathered at the monastery he established at Eihei-ji eventually organized themselves into a formal school. The second abbot of Eihei-ji, {{ill|Koyun Kaizō|ja|孤雲懐奘|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Koyun Kaizō|qq=}}, recorded Dōgen’s teachings in the “Zōbutsu Genjōzu Suibun-ki,” and later, in the late Kamakura period, {{ill|Eisanjō Shōshin|ja|瑩山紹瑾|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisanjō Shōshin|qq=}} established the Sōtō Zen organization in the Hokuriku region based on the teachings of Dōgen.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} (For further details on Dōgen’s doctrine of “shūshō ittō,” see the section “Dōgen and Sōtō Zen” below.) {{File:Eiheiji15s4592.jpg|300px|right|thumb|Eihei-ji: The stair-like cloister}} Dōgen advocated the “non-reliance on written words” (furitsumonji) and taught that one must discard all conceptual thinking and engage in zazen with single-minded dedication (shikan taizan) in order to let one’s true self manifest – a practice which, he declared, is the very act of being a Buddha. Although he also performed invocations and prayers, these were in line with his overall demand to strip away the “excesses” of conventional Buddhist practice, and this very insistence led to ever more severe persecution from the monks of Enryaku-ji.{{ill|Gomi (2000)|ja|五味（2000）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gomi (2000)|qq=}}{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Dōgen’s major treatise, the “Shōbō Genjō” (correct Dharma Eye), originally written in Japanese, remains renowned for its ontological, temporal, and linguistic insights and is widely regarded as one of the masterpieces of religious and philosophical writing in the Japanese language.The title “Shōbō Genjō” signifies the secret Dharma realized through the “correct Dharma Eye.” (Murakami (1981) p.97)Regarding his treatment of time, the section “Yūji” in volume 75 of the work is often compared to the philosophies of Martin Heidegger and Henri Bergson. [https://1000ya.isis.ne.jp/0988.html Reference: Matsuoka Masakō’s Thousand Nights, Thousand Volumes: “Shōbō Genjō”] Dōgen’s carefully wrought language and style have set a high standard in Japanese religious and philosophical discourse.{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.101-106|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}}{{ill|Seigō Dōgen|ja|松岡正剛の千夜千冊『正法眼蔵』|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seigō Dōgen|qq=}} In the opening of the “Gensen Kōan” section of “Shōbō Genjō,” Dōgen expounds: “To study the Buddha’s way means to study oneself; to study oneself means to forget oneself. To forget oneself means to be validated by all phenomena; and to be validated by all phenomena means to have one’s body and mind, as well as that of others, transcended.”{{ill|Bitoh (2000)|ja|尾藤（2000）pp.101-106|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bitoh (2000)|qq=}} In other words, learning the Buddha’s way is equivalent to knowing oneself – and to know oneself is to cast off one’s attachments, thereby allowing the true nature of all things to be revealed, leading to the dissolution of the boundary between self and other and thus to enlightenment. Dōgen’s ideas on “shūshō ittō” (the oneness of practice and realization) eventually spread widely among local warriors, and his teaching that every aspect of life is a form of practice came to be especially embraced by the common people. It should also be noted that during this period, itinerant monks – not only of the Zen school but also from the other schools such as the Vinaya school and Jishū – frequently traveled between regions. In the case of Zen, these itinerant monks often established lodging facilities known as “Dangai” to accommodate their travels.{{ill|Harada (2009)|ja|原田（2009）p.4|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Harada (2009)|qq=}} == Renewal of “Old Buddhism” == Although “New Buddhism,” which emphasized faith and practice, gradually spread among the warriors and commoners, the traditional Buddhist groups – such as the Southern Six Sects, Tendai, and Shingon – continued to wield significant social influence. In particular, the Tendai school retained its great power and often collaborated with the secular authorities (the “Gonmon” system) to suppress the new Buddhist movements.{{ill|Kanemitsu|ja|権門体制|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanemitsu|qq=}} However, spurred by the vigorous activities of the “New Buddhism,” even within the realm of “Old Buddhism” there arose a spirit of self-criticism and calls for reform. (Note that, as will be discussed later, it was not until the Muromachi and Sengoku periods that the reform movements of “New Buddhism” acquired sufficient social power to effect real change.) {| border="1" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="3" style="text-align:left" |- |- style="background:#efefef;" | style="font-weight:bold" | Sect | style="font-weight:bold" | Monk | style="font-weight:bold" | Notable Acts |- | style="background:#efefef;font-weight:bold" rowspan="1" | {{ill|Hossō Buddhism|ja|法相宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hossō Buddhism|qq=}} | {{ill|Jōkei (Gedatsudō)|ja|貞慶 (解脱)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkei (Gedatsudō)|qq=}}
{{ill|1155|ja|1155年|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1155|qq=}} – {{ill|1213|ja|1213rd year|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/1213|qq=}} | Criticized the moral decay of the monks at {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōfuku-ji|qq=}} and retreated to {{ill|Kasagi-yama|ja|笠置山|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasagi-yama|qq=}} where he dedicated himself to the maintenance and dissemination of the precepts, and launched attacks against Hōnen’s exclusive nembutsu teaching. |- | style="background:#efefef;font-weight:bold" rowspan="1" | {{ill|Huayan Buddhism|ja|華厳宗|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Huayan Buddhism|qq=}} | {{ill|Myōei|ja|明恵|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōei|qq=}}
