{{ill|1281|en|1281|WD=Q5537|lt=1281}} – {{ill|1356|en|1356|WD=Q6130|lt=1356}} | Influenced by the activities of Eisō and others, he launched a movement to “revive” the precepts. He participated in the overthrow of the Kamakura shogunate under Emperor Go-Daigo and was responsible for editing the “Taiheiki.” |- |} === Hossō Buddhism === Born in Kyoto and regarded as the reviver of Hossō Buddhism, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|en|Jōkei (monk)|WD=Q11634518|lt=Jōkei (Gedatsudō)}} (1155–1213) studied Hossō doctrine and the Vinaya under his uncle {{ill|Kakuken|ja|覚憲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kakuken|1=Kakuken|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11630329}} at {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|en|Kōfuku-ji|WD=Q1070863|lt=Kōfuku-ji}}. However, disillusioned by the secularization of Kōfuku-ji, which had become dominated by the manor lords, he left the temple and retreated to the mountains of Yamashiro at {{ill|Kasagi-dera|ja|笠置寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasagi-dera|1=Kasagi-dera|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11599950}}, where he dedicated himself to the revival of the precepts. In {{ill|1205|en|1205|WD=Q5229|lt=1205}} (the 2nd year of Genkyū) he issued the “Kōfuku-ji Sōjō” condemning Pure Land Buddhism, which in turn helped trigger the persecution of Hōnen. In {{ill|1208|en|1208|WD=Q5238|lt=1208}} (the 2nd year of Shōgen) Jōkei transferred his activities to the re-established Kaizumi-sanji.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}} Jōkei and his contemporary, {{ill|Ryōben (Ryōhaku)|ja|良遍|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ryōben (Ryōhaku)|1=Ryōben (Ryōhaku)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11614430}} of the Hossō school, rejected the traditional “five natures” doctrine (which held that some humans lack Buddha-nature) and instead taught that the concept of “no-nature” was merely a skillful means, asserting that all beings possess Buddha-nature.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}} Jōkei’s radical reinterpretation – which went so far as to be seen as self-denial – set forth a pioneering vision for Hossō Buddhism.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}} The five-storied pagoda at Kaizumi-sanji was built by Jōkei’s disciple {{ill|Kakushin|ja|覚真|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kakushin|qq=}} in memory of his master and has been designated a National Treasure. === Huayan Buddhism === {{File:Semuiji Myoue.jpg|130px|right|thumb|Portrait of {{ill|Myōe|en|Myōe|WD=Q2026000|lt=Myōei}} engaging in seated meditation (a National Treasure)}} The reviver of Huayan Buddhism, {{ill|Myōe|en|Myōe|WD=Q2026000|lt=Myōei}} (1173–1232), was born as a son in {{ill|Kii Province|en|Kii Province|WD=Q864053|lt=Kii Province}} and is known by the name “Myōei Shōnin.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Myōei received patronage from both the retired Emperor {{ill|Go-Toba|ja|後鳥羽上皇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go-Toba|1=Go-Toba|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q316658}} and {{ill|Hōjō Yasutoki|en|Hōjō Yasutoki|WD=Q1188359|lt=Hojo Yasutoki}}.During the Jōkyū War, Hojo Yasutoki, who served as the commander of the shogunate forces and later became the first Rokuhara Tandai, is said to have been influenced in his formulation of the “Onaribai Shikime” by Myōei’s thought. In {{ill|1188|en|1188|WD=Q19732|lt=1188}} (the 4th year of Bunji), Myōei took ordination under {{ill|Jōkaku|ja|上覚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jōkaku|1=Jōkaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360115}}, receiving precepts at Tōdai-ji; after studying Huayan doctrine at Sonshō-in, he renounced the world at the age of 21 and left Tōdai-ji. In {{ill|1206|en|1206|WD=Q5230|lt=1206}} (the 1st year of Ken'ei), by order of the retired Emperor {{ill|Go-Toba|ja|後鳥羽上皇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Go-Toba|1=Go-Toba|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q316658}}, Myōei established the temple {{ill|Kōzan-ji|en|Kōzan-ji|WD=Q986750|lt=Takayama-dera}} in Tsugao, northern Kyoto, and issued the treatise “Sai Gyarin,” in which he refuted Hōnen’s exclusive nembutsu teaching. Throughout his life, he devoted himself to the restoration of the Buddha’s precepts.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} === Vinaya Buddhism === Within Vinaya Buddhism, the monk {{ill|Jinsetsu (Gazen)|ja|俊芿 (我禅)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jinsetsu (Gazen)|qq=}} (1166–1227) returned from Song China after studying the precepts, and re-established {{ill|Sennyū-ji|en|Sennyū-ji|WD=Q1060966|lt=Senyū-ji}} in Kyoto – creating a training center that combined Tendai, Shingon, Zen, and Vinaya learning. He is sometimes credited with introducing Song Confucianism (later Zhu Xi’s teachings) to Japan.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）pp.106-108|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} The revival of Vinaya Buddhism is further exemplified by {{ill|Eisō (Shien)|ja|叡尊 (思円)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisō (Shien)|qq=}} (1201–1290), who was born in {{ill|Yamato Province|en|Yamato Province|WD=Q907495|lt=Yamato Province}} to a family of monks from Kōfuku-ji. At the age of 17, in {{ill|1217|en|1217|WD=Q5379|lt=1217}} (the 5th year of Kenpō), he was ordained at Daigo-ji in Kyoto and received precepts at Tōdai-ji soon after.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} In {{ill|1236|en|1236|WD=Q5427|lt=1236}} (the 2nd year of Kaje), together with associates from Kōfuku-ji including {{ill|Kakusei|ja|覚盛|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kakusei|1=Kakusei|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11630350}}, he vowed before the bodhisattva of Guanyin at the Tōdai-ji Lotus Hall, pledging not only to pursue his own enlightenment but also to work for the salvation of others. Eisei later re-established the old {{ill|Saidaiji|ja|西大寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saidaiji|1=Saidaiji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q81436}} in Yamato and devoted himself to a rigorous restoration of the precepts. He also oversaw a variety of public works – including road and port construction as well as bridge building – and was actively involved in charitable activities such as the rescue of outcasts and the poor.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.150-151|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}}{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.7-17|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} It is said that Eisei personally conferred precepts on 1,694 monks and over 60,000 lay devotees.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}}{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.168-181|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Eisei established new ordination platforms at both {{ill|Saidaiji|ja|西大寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saidaiji|1=Saidaiji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q81436}} and {{ill|Tōshōdai-ji|en|Tōshōdai-ji|WD=Q973175|lt=Tang Zhaotai-ji}} for monks who had received state ordination in the official circles, and also opened the ordination path for tosses, leaving a profound impact on Kamakura society.{{ill|Amino (1997)|ja|網野（1997）pp.150-151|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amino (1997)|qq=}} {{File:Kitayama-Juhachikento01.jpg|right|250px|thumb|The historical site {{ill|Kitayama Jūhachikento|en|Kitayama Jūhachikento|WD=Q11401444|lt=Kitayama Jūhakkando}} (Nara), established by Ninshō (Ryōkan) for the salvation of outcasts}} {{File:Monju crossing the sea.jpg|200px|right|thumb|National Treasure “Silk Manuscript Colored Monju Crossing the Sea” (13th century, housed at {{ill|Daigo-ji|en|Daigo-ji|WD=Q1157535|lt=Daigo-ji}}}} Another noted Vinaya scholar was {{ill|Enchō (Entō)|ja|円照|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enchō (Entō)|1=Enchō (Entō)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q56353646}} (1221–1277) and his disciple {{ill|Gyōnen|en|Gyōnen|WD=Q3122771|lt=Gyōzen}} (1240–1321). Particularly, Gyōzen, who was well-versed in the Huayan Sutra, wrote extensively on the history of Buddhism in India, China, and Japan, and his work “Hassō Kōyō” is considered highly significant in Japanese Buddhist historiography.{{ill|Oosumi (1989)|ja|大隅（1989）p.210|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Oosumi (1989)|qq=}}In “Hassō Kōyō,” the term “Hassō” refers to the eight sects, namely the six Southern sects (Nara Buddhism) plus the two Heian sects (Tendai and Shingon), as defined also in the “Kōfuku-ji Sōjō.” === Shingon Buddhism === At {{ill|Mount Kōya|en|Mount Kōya|WD=Q535065|lt=Koyasan}}, during the late Heian period, the monk {{ill|Kakuban|en|Kakuban|WD=Q1676043|lt=Kakuban}} (1095–1143) emerged and established a major institution called Daitenbōin in the mountain, engaging in widespread propagation of the faith among the common people. However, due to conflicts with {{ill|Kongōbu-ji|en|Kongōbu-ji|WD=Q1203429|lt=Kongōbu-ji}}, he withdrew to {{ill|Negoro-ji|en|Negoro-ji|WD=Q1552446|lt=Nemoto-ji (Negarai)}} in Kii Province.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} Kakuban subsequently systematized the diverse practices of Shingon Buddhism, giving rise to the Daitenbōin lineage. A prolonged conflict ensued between the faction from Kongōbu-ji (the honzen side) and the Daitenbōin faction (the in-院 side) that traced its lineage to Kakuban. During the mid-Kamakura period, the monk {{ill|Raiyū|ja|頼瑜|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raiyū|1=Raiyu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11665023}} (1226–1304) became prominent in Daitenbōin activities; however, facing increasing pressure from the Kongōbu-ji faction, in {{ill|1286|en|1286|WD=Q5548|lt=1286}} (the 9th year of Kōan) Raiyū shifted the Daitenbōin base to Negarai Enmyō-ji in Negarai and from Koyasan separated to establish the Shin-gi Shingon sect – which emphasized the “power body” (加持法身) of Dainichi Nyorai.{{ill|Murakami (1981)|ja|村上（1981）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami (1981)|qq=}} === Tendai Buddhism === Born in Ōmi, {{ill|Enkan (Empaku)|ja|円観 (恵鎮)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enkan (Empaku)|qq=}} (1281–1356) was ordained at Enryaku-ji in {{ill|1295|en|1295|WD=Q5560|lt=1295}} (the 3rd year of Einin) and received the official monk name “Iyōbō Dōsei.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} In {{ill|1303|en|1303|WD=Q5614|lt=1303}} (the 1st year of Kayogen) he briefly became a Zen monk but returned to Kurotani the following year; around {{ill|1305|en|1305|WD=Q5624|lt=1305}} (the 3rd year of Kayogen), following the guidance of his master {{ill|Kōen|ja|興円|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōen|1=Kōen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11613341}}, he once again renounced worldly life and subsequently worked with his master to advocate for the upholding of the Tendai precepts (enkai). This movement to restore the precepts was influenced by the activities of southern figures such as Eisō.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Enkan also played an important role as the head abbot of Tōdai-ji and in the reconstruction of {{ill|Hosshō-ji|en|Hosshō-ji|WD=Q3141015|lt=Hōshō-ji}}, and even served as the chief editor of the “Taiheiki.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} He participated in Emperor Go-Daigo’s movement to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate and, after the collapse of the Kenmu Restoration, came under the patronage of {{ill|Ashikaga Takauji|en|Ashikaga Takauji|WD=Q297107|lt=Ashikaga Takauji}} and is credited with involvement in the drafting of the Kenmu Shikimoku. In his numerous writings on the precepts, Enkan is considered a central figure in Tendai doctrinal revival. === Relationship Between “Old Buddhism” and “New Buddhism” === Thus, while “Old Buddhism” emphasized the revival of the precepts and the state’s role in safeguarding the nation – with little concern for the salvation of the common people – “New Buddhism” (especially the nembutsu sects) were characterized by a vigorous rejection of strict precepts. The aforementioned persecution in the 1st year of Shōgen was triggered by such doctrinal differences. On the other hand, even within what is termed “Old Buddhism,” there emerged new movements inspired by the six new sects. Specifically, figures such as {{ill|Myōe|en|Myōe|WD=Q2026000|lt=Myōei}} of Huayan Buddhism, {{ill|Gyōnen|en|Gyōnen|WD=Q3122771|lt=Gyōzen}}, and {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|en|Jōkei (monk)|WD=Q11634518|lt=Jōkei (Gedatsudō)}} of Hossō, as well as {{ill|Kakuban|en|Kakuban|WD=Q1676043|lt=Kakuban}} of Shingon, established institutions that carried out extensive social projects. A key issue among scholars has been whether these activities should be simply categorized as “Old Buddhism” or rather as part of “New Buddhism.” === On the Establishment of the “Shingon-Ritsuryū” Organization === {{main|Shingon-Ritsuryū Theory|顕密体制論}} Matsuo Takeshi and others view the most important elements of Kamakura New Buddhism as “independence from the state” and “salvation of the individual.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.149-166|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} In this context, later the group known as “Shingon-Ritsuryū” was the first among the new sects to establish its own ordination platform in place of the state’s kaidan, initiate its own ordination process, and conduct extensive social work – including the ordination of women (bhikkhunīs) who had been previously refused ordination by the state – thus focusing on the salvation of individuals. This organization is regarded by many as one of the elements of Kamakura New Buddhism, much like the six sects founded by Hōnen, Shinran, Eisai, Dōgen, Nichiren, and Ippen.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}Eisō, for example, conceptualized the precepts and esoteric teachings (Shingon) as two pillars, saying they are “like the sun and the moon” (if precepts are the sun, then esoteric teachings are the moon) – a clear indication of their inseparability. (松尾（1995）p.159) Additionally, scholars such as {{ill|Heiyagō Kōgyō|ja|平雅行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heiyagō Kōgyō|1=Masayuki Taira|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11483776}} have noted that the school of Eisō and his followers (the Nishida-ryū) in many ways differ from traditional Vinaya Buddhism in their attitude toward the precepts and in the composition of their lay memberships, thereby possessing the intrinsic qualities to be regarded as “the progenitors of Kamakura New Buddhism.” === The Ienaga–Inoue Theory === The views of Ienaga Saburō and Inoue Kōtei have long been widely accepted. According to their theory, the six sects founded by Hōnen, Shinran, Eisai, Dōgen, Nichiren, and Ippen were “Kamakura New Buddhism” – characterized by their emphasis on “selective practice” (sentaku), “exclusive practice” (senjū), ease of practice (igyō), lay-based orientation, and the salvation of even the sinful – which opened the door to salvation for a broad range of people, transcending social classes and status.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} == The “Eight-Sect System” and “Exoteric–Esoteric System” Theory == {{main|Eight-Sect System Theory|顕密体制論}} In 1969 the Buddhist historian {{ill|Tamura Ensui|ja|田村圓澄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamura Ensui|1=Enchō Tamura|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11576891}} first proposed what came to be known as the “Eight-Sect System Theory.” This theory, based on the insights of Ienaga, Inoue, and others, reinterpreted the establishment of Kamakura New Buddhism as the rise of a popular Buddhism centered on individual salvation in contrast to the aristocratic, ritual-based “nation-protecting Buddhism” of ancient times.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）pp.92-94|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} In his essay “Historical Evaluation of Kamakura Buddhism,” Tamura noted that the phrase “the eight sects united in common purpose” found in the “Kōfuku-ji Sōjō” (an official document) indicated that the eight sects (the Southern Six plus the two Heian sects) had united in their opposition to Hōnen’s teachings in order to defend their own vested interests, thereby coalescing an ancient Buddhist order that he named the “Eight-Sect System.”{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）pp.91-92|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} Based on the work of Ienaga and Inoue, the conventional equation of “Old Buddhism” with ancient Buddhism and “New Buddhism” with medieval Buddhism – which has dominated the scholarly consensus – is now being reexamined. In particular, the Buddhist organizations established by figures such as Eisō and Ninshō have been argued to contain elements that warrant their inclusion among “New Buddhism.” === On the “Tosses” (Donses) as a Perspective === More recently, scholar {{ill|Matsuo Takeshi|ja|松尾剛次|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo Takeshi|1=Kenji Matsuo|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11529581}} has advanced a new analysis based on distinguishing between the “official priesthood” (kan-sō) and the “tosses” (donses) – monks who left the state-sanctioned world to devote themselves to individual salvation. According to Matsuo, the true “Kamakura New Buddhism” should be understood as those sects founded by such tosses, and on that basis even figures traditionally classified under “Old Buddhism” such as Myōei and Eisō may be reinterpreted as belonging to the same “new” category.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Matsuo’s perspective is summarized in the table below: {|class="wikitable" cellspacing="0" ! Item !! Explanation according to Matsuo |- | New Buddhism || Buddhism whose founders are tosses – including Hōnen, Shinran, Nichiren, Eisō, Dōgen, Ippen, Myōei, Enchō, and Enkan – emphasizing individual salvation. |- | Old Buddhism || Buddhism practiced by the official priesthood (kan-sō), ordained by the Emperor for the safeguarding of the nation. |- | Features of New Buddhism || A “personal” religion prioritizing individual salvation, with a strong emphasis on the veneration of the founder. |- | Features of Old Buddhism || A communal religion oriented toward the protection of the nation through ritual prayer. |- | Medieval Buddhism || Classified as New Buddhism. |- | Target Audience || Urban “individuals.” |- | Relationship with Socioeconomic History || Interprets the manor system as a medieval institution, and the temples that functioned as manor lords as similarly medieval. |- |} {{File:Ippen Biography 3.jpg|300px|right|thumb|An illustrated scroll depicting the practice of “dancing nembutsu” from the {{ill|Ippen Shōnin Eiden|ja|一遍上人絵伝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ippen Shōnin Eiden|1=Ippen Shōnin Eden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2904124}} (a National Treasure)}} According to Matsuo, with the exception of Ippen – who, although not having had official ordination, was mythologized as having studied at Enryaku-ji and received ordination there – all the founders of what became known as Kamakura New Buddhism initially received state ordination. However, through their struggles with, and eventual break from, the official priesthood, they forged new paths. Matsuo argues that while the “Old Buddhism” was characterized by state ordination (typically with white robes under the ritsuryō system), the “New Buddhism” developed its own distinctive entry ritual and, for example, adopted black robes to signify the transcendence of notions of “impurity” and social status.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.50-60|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} The color of the robes thus symbolized the monk’s self‐conception. Furthermore, Matsuo contends that whereas official priests – burdened by the obligation to serve the court and avoid “impurity” – were restricted in their activities (such as ministering to women, outcasts, or conducting funeral rites), the tosses, free from state privilege, were able to engage fully in such activities. This, he asserts, is the essence of what should be recognized as “New Buddhism.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.120-141|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} === On the Validity of the “New Buddhism” Concept === On the other hand, scholar {{ill|Heiyagō Kōgyō|ja|平雅行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heiyagō Kōgyō|1=Masayuki Taira|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11483776}} has expressed reservations about the validity of the analytical term “Kamakura New Buddhism.” While figures such as Jōkei and Ryōben indeed developed bold new doctrines that departed markedly from traditional teachings, and while groups like Eisō’s reformed Vinaya school exhibited distinct characteristics, Heiyagō argues that Nichiren’s aims – which were ultimately directed toward a revival of Tendai – suggest that his school might be more accurately classified within the framework of “Old Buddhism’s revival.” He further points out that the criteria for differentiating “New Buddhism” from “Old Buddhism” actually reflect developments in the Edo period rather than those of the Kamakura period.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}}Some scholars have even proposed the term “Edo New Buddhism” for those sects that were recognized as independent during the Edo period. Moreover, Heiyagō maintains that ancient Buddhism had already undergone profound transformations from the 9th to the 10th centuries – with the integration of various sects and the emergence of a distinctly personal religious faith – such that even in the mid-Heian period there were numerous accounts of salvation for sinners and women, as well as petitions by “rogue monks” that displayed an element of popular mobilization.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}} Thus, Heiyagō argues that the conventional concept of “Kamakura New Buddhism” – which overemphasizes the influence of figures such as Shinran and Nichiren – is more a projection of later (early modern) sectarian arrangements onto the Kamakura period rather than an accurate reflection of its internal dynamics.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}}For example, some have suggested that “New Buddhism” might more appropriately be termed “Edo New Buddhism” given that its distinct social role was not fully established until the Sengoku period. == Kamakura Buddhism Theory == === The Proposal of the “Old Buddhism” vs. “New Buddhism” Concept === The very notion of dividing Kamakura Buddhism into “Old Buddhism” and “New Buddhism” is a relatively modern interpretation that first appeared in the pioneering work of {{ill|Senshō Murakami|en|Senshō Murakami|WD=Q2645939|lt=Murakami Sensē}}, who in the Meiji period (1898–1899) published the “Outline of Japanese Buddhist History.” In that work, the expression “New Buddhism” was used to include not only the reformist movements of figures such as Myōei but also to explain the reforms undertaken by those Buddhist groups that did not participate in these movements by referring to them as “Conventional Buddhism” or “Ancient Schools.” Entering the Taishō period and continuing into the Shōwa period, the six sects founded by Hōnen, Shinran, Eisai, Dōgen, Nichiren, and Ippen came to be differentiated from the pre-existing sects. The view that these six constitute “Kamakura New Buddhism” – with its hallmarks of selective practice, exclusive reliance, ease of practice (in contrast to strict precepts), lay orientation, and the salvation even of sinners – remained the dominant orthodoxy through the postwar period, championed by scholars such as {{ill|Saburō Ienaga|en|Saburō Ienaga|WD=Q909366|lt=Ienaga Saburō}} and {{ill|Inoue Kōtei|ja|井上光貞|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoue Kōtei|1=Mitsusada Inoue|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11372857}}. On the other hand, even within what has traditionally been called “Old Buddhism” (for instance, the Nara and Heian schools), new movements emerged that were inspired by the six new sects. Specifically, the Buddhist activities of figures such as Myōei of Huayan, Gyōzen, and Jōkei of Hossō, as well as the temple organizations established by the Shingon sect’s Kakuban and by the Vinaya schools of Eisō and his disciple Ninshō, have led some to question whether it is entirely appropriate to label them simply as “Old Buddhism.” === On the “Shingon-Ritsuryū” Organization === {{main|Shingon-Ritsuryū|顕密体制論}} {{ill|Matsuo Takeshi|ja|松尾剛次|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo Takeshi|1=Kenji Matsuo|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11529581}} argued that the two key elements essential for the emergence of a popular, people-oriented Buddhism – namely, independence from the state and the salvation of the individual – were present only when a Buddhist movement broke away from aristocratic Buddhism. In his view, the group later known as “Shingon-Ritsuryū” was the first among the new sects to establish its own ordination system (in place of the state’s kaidan) and to launch its own ordination process through social work aimed at rescuing the outcasts and those who had hitherto been refused ordination by the state (including women). Thus, he asserted that Shingon-Ritsuryū should be regarded as one of the expressions of Kamakura New Buddhism.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.149-166|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}Eisō argued that precepts and esoteric teachings are inseparable, likening them to “the sun and the moon.” (松尾（1995）p.159) === The Ienaga–Inoue Perspective === The theories of {{ill|Saburō Ienaga|en|Saburō Ienaga|WD=Q909366|lt=Ienaga Saburō}} and {{ill|Inoue Kōtei|ja|井上光貞|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoue Kōtei|1=Mitsusada Inoue|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11372857}} – which treat the six sects established by Hōnen, Shinran, Eisai, Dōgen, Nichiren, and Ippen as “Kamakura New Buddhism” characterized by selective practice, exclusive reliance, ease of practice, lay orientation, and the salvation of even sinners – have enjoyed overwhelming support among scholars.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} Ienaga’s groundbreaking work (published in 1947 in a series of essays in “Studies in Medieval Buddhist Thought”) argued that because the Tendai and Shingon schools of Heian Buddhism had functioned essentially as “nation-protecting Buddhism” with little regard for the common people, the innovative, people-oriented approach of “Kamakura New Buddhism” was truly revolutionary.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} Inoue’s theoretical work, “A Study on the Formation of Japanese Pure Land Buddhism” (1956), further reinforced this view.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）pp.94-96|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} === The “Eight-Sect System” and “Exoteric–Esoteric System” Theories === {{main|Eight-Sect System Theory|顕密体制論}} In 1969, Buddhist historian {{ill|Tamura Ensui|ja|田村圓澄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamura Ensui|1=Enchō Tamura|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11576891}} first proposed what became known as the “Eight-Sect System Theory.” This theory, based on the insights of Ienaga, Inoue, and others, reinterprets the establishment of Kamakura Buddhism as the rise of a popular, individually oriented Buddhism in contrast to the aristocratic, ritualistic, state-supported Buddhism of ancient times.{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）pp.92-94|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} Tamura noted in his paper “Historical Evaluation of Kamakura Buddhism” that the phrase “the eight sects united as one” in the “Kōfuku-ji Sōjō” (a document of the traditional Buddhist establishment) suggests that the eight sects (the Southern Six and the two Heian sects) united in their opposition to Hōnen’s teachings out of self-interest, and he termed this ancient Buddhist order the “Eight-Sect System.”{{ill|Sotēn (1991)|ja|佐藤弘夫（1991）pp.91-92|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sotēn (1991)|qq=}} Based on the consensus reached by Ienaga, Inoue, and others, the equation of “Old Buddhism” with ancient Buddhism and “New Buddhism” with medieval Buddhism is now being reexamined.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} === The “Tosses” Perspective === More recently, {{ill|Matsuo Takeshi|ja|松尾剛次|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo Takeshi|1=Kenji Matsuo|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11529581}} has proposed a new framework by distinguishing between the “official priesthood” (kan-sō), whose members were ordained by the Emperor to pray for the nation, and the “tosses” (donses) – those monks who broke away from that system to devote themselves to individual salvation. According to Matsuo, the true “Kamakura New Buddhism” should be defined by those groups whose founders were tosses. In this context, even figures traditionally classified as “Old Buddhism” such as Myōei, Eisō, and Enkan may well be regarded as belonging to New Buddhism.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} His view is summarized in the table below: {|class="wikitable" cellspacing="0" ! Item !! Explanation according to Matsuo |- | New Buddhism || Buddhism whose founders (Hōnen, Shinran, Nichiren, Eisō, Dōgen, Ippen, Myōei, Enchō, and Enkan) were originally ordained but later broke from the official priesthood, emphasizing individual salvation. |- | Old Buddhism || Buddhism practiced by the official priesthood (ordained by the Emperor for national protection). |- | Features of New Buddhism || A “personal” religion that prioritizes individual salvation and founder veneration. |- | Features of Old Buddhism || A communal religion primarily focused on national prayers for protection. |- | Medieval Buddhism || Identified with New Buddhism. |- | Target Audience || Urban individuals. |- | Relationship with Socioeconomic History || Considers the manor system to be a medieval institution and regards temples as akin to local feudal lords. |- |} {{File:Ippen Biography 3.jpg|300px|right|thumb|An illustrated scroll depicting the practice of “dancing nembutsu” from the {{ill|Ippen Shōnin Eiden|ja|一遍上人絵伝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ippen Shōnin Eiden|1=Ippen Shōnin Eden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2904124}} (a National Treasure)}} Matsuo points out that, with the single exception of Ippen (who, despite never having undergone formal state ordination, was mythologized as if he had studied and been ordained at Enryaku-ji), all of the founders of what came to be known as Kamakura New Buddhism were initially formally ordained as state priests. However, through conflicts and eventual separation from the official priesthood, they ultimately established the paths they later advocated. Matsuo further notes that whereas the “Old Buddhism” was characterized by state ordination (with white robes under the ritsuryō system), the “New Buddhism” developed its own distinct initiation ritual – for example, by adopting black robes that signified a transcendence of impurity and class distinctions.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.50-60|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Furthermore, Matsuo emphasizes that while official priests, owing to their privileged status and duty to serve the court, were constrained from ministering to women, outcasts, or engaging in funerary rites, the tosses who chose to wear black robes were free from such restrictions and could fully engage in such activities. He contends that this freedom of action is the core of what should be recognized as “New Buddhism.”{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}}{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.120-141|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} === On the Validity of the “New Buddhism” Concept === Conversely, {{ill|Heiyagō Kōgyō|ja|平雅行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heiyagō Kōgyō|1=Masayuki Taira|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11483776}} has raised doubts about the analytical term “Kamakura New Buddhism.” While figures such as Jōkei and Ryōben indeed advanced bold doctrines that broke with traditional teachings, and while groups like Eisō’s reformed Vinaya organization exhibited new characteristics, Heiyagō argues that Nichiren’s aspirations – which were aimed at reviving Tendai Buddhism – indicate that his school might more appropriately be categorized within the framework of “Old Buddhism’s revival.” He further suggests that the criteria for distinguishing “New Buddhism” were in fact formulated during the Edo period, reflecting later developments rather than the realities of the Kamakura period.{{PDFlink|[http://www.jikkyo.co.jp/contents/download/7851663520 平雅行「中世史像の変化と鎌倉仏教(2)」]}} == Footnotes == === Note === {{Reflist|group="Note"}} === References === {{Reflist|3}} == References == * [[ja:鎌倉仏教]] [[ja:鎌倉仏教]] [[ja:鎌倉仏教]] [[ja:鎌倉仏教]] '''Kamakura Buddhism''' (鎌倉仏教) Kamakura Buddhism is a term used to refer collectively to the Buddhist sects of Japan that emerged newly from the late {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian Period}} to the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura Period}}. In some contexts it is also applied to denote the entire spectrum of Buddhism during the Kamakura period – including the revival of the old Buddhism of the Nara and Heian periods – although no clear definition exists. Because of this ambiguity, some distinguish only those sects that spread newly by calling them “{{ill|Kamakura Buddhism|lt=Kamakura Buddhism|lt=Kamakura New Buddhism|ja|鎌倉新仏教|lt=Kamakura Buddhism|lt=Kamakura New Buddhism|lt_ja=鎌倉新仏教|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamakura New Buddhism|qq=}}”. In that case the term refers to the six sects founded respectively by: * {{ill|Hōnen|en|Hōnen|WD=Q507980|lt=Hōnen}}, founder of {{ill|Jōdo-shū|en|Jōdo-shū|WD=Q912208|lt=Pure Land Buddhism}}; * {{ill|Shinran|en|Shinran|WD=Q512934|lt=Shinran}}, founder of {{ill|Jōdo Shinshū|en|Jōdo Shinshū|WD=Q912221|lt=True Pure Land Buddhism}}; * {{ill|Eisai|ja|栄西|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisai|1=Eisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q366128}}, founder of {{ill|Rinzai school|en|Rinzai school|WD=Q639625|lt=Rinzai Zen}}; * {{ill|Dōgen|en|Dōgen|WD=Q318064|lt=Dōgen}}, founder of {{ill|Sōtō|en|Sōtō|WD=Q749085|lt=Sōtō Zen}}; * {{ill|Nichiren|1=Nichiren|2=ja|3=日蓮|4=ko|5=니치렌|6=de|7=Nichiren|8=es|9=Nichiren|10=fr|11=Nichiren|12=it|13=Nichiren|14=nl|15=Nichiren|16=no|17=Nichiren|lt=Nichiren|WD=Q311478en|Nichiren|1=Nichiren|2=ja|3=日蓮|4=ko|5=니치렌|6=de|7=Nichiren|8=es|9=Nichiren|10=fr|11=Nichiren|12=it|13=Nichiren|14=nl|15=Nichiren|16=no|17=Nichiren|lt=Nichiren|WD=Q311478WD=Q311478|lt=Nichiren}}, founder of {{ill|Nichiren-shū|en|Nichiren-shū|WD=Q206611|lt=Nichiren Buddhism}}; and * {{ill|Ippen|en|Ippen|WD=Q1056232|lt=Ippen}}, founder of the {{ill|Ji-shu|en|Ji-shu|WD=Q696966|lt=Jishū}}. Until the Heian period, Buddhism was essentially the religion of the Emperor and the aristocracy, reserved for those of high status. In contrast, the characteristic of Kamakura New Buddhism was its “ease of faith” – in the background of the Mappō thought (the belief that the degenerate age began in 1052) and amid an era marked by frequent earthquakes, famines, epidemics, and the looming threat of two Mongol invasions, as well as as many as fifty era name changes (of which thirty were “disaster era changes”) during a time of intense suffering among the people. Consequently, these sects spread widely among not only the commoners but also the warrior class. The distinctive teachings of each sect can be broadly divided into three features: nembutsu (reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha), daimoku (chanting the title of the Lotus Sutra), and zazen (seated meditation). Discussions regarding the term “Kamakura New Buddhism” are varied among scholars (see below the section “Kamakura Buddhism Theory”). == Overview == {{File:Illustrated biography of priest Hōnen 2.jpg|300px|left|thumb|The life of {{ill|Hōnen|en|Hōnen|WD=Q507980|lt=Hōnen}} as depicted in the picture scroll of his biography (a National Treasure) showing his efforts for women’s salvation}} During the Kamakura period, while the state undertook projects such as the reconstruction of temples in the southern capital (starting with {{ill|Tōdai-ji|en|Tōdai-ji|WD=Q460367|lt=Tōdai-ji}}) and other temples in Nara, from the mid-12th century to the 13th century, new Buddhist sects emerged in response to the demands of newly rising warriors and farmers. These included the founders of {{ill|Jōdo-shū|en|Jōdo-shū|WD=Q912208|lt=Pure Land Buddhism}}, {{ill|Jōdo Shinshū|en|Jōdo Shinshū|WD=Q912221|lt=True Pure Land Buddhism}}, {{ill|Ji-shu|en|Ji-shu|WD=Q696966|lt=Jishū}}, {{ill|Nichiren-shū|en|Nichiren-shū|WD=Q206611|lt=Nichiren Buddhism}}, {{ill|Rinzai school|en|Rinzai school|WD=Q639625|lt=Rinzai Zen}}, and {{ill|Sōtō|en|Sōtō|WD=Q749085|lt=Sōtō Zen}} (although the Pure Land sect was in fact founded in the late Heian period, it is generally included among Kamakura New Buddhism). All six sects had founders who, in one way or another, had studied under the influence of the older Buddhist traditions (for example, at Enryaku-ji of the Tendai school). The first four emerged from within the framework of “old Buddhism” while the latter two were newly imported from China. Although these six sects differ in their doctrines and historical circumstances of formation, they share a common standpoint in that they do not require the strict precepts, scholarly study, or costly temple-building demanded by old Buddhism; rather, they teach that salvation is accessible to laypeople solely through faith. In contrast, on the side of “old Buddhism” (including the six Nara schools, Tendai, and Shingon), efforts were made – beginning in the Nara period when the Chinese monk {{ill|Jianzhen|en|Jianzhen|WD=Q714061|lt=Ganjin}} transmitted the precepts to Japan – to maintain and disseminate these precepts, while also contributing to various social projects.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.19-47|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} Moreover, in both “new Buddhism” and “old Buddhism,” a significant role was played by the so-called "tosses" (脱世僧) – Buddhist monks who, having freed themselves from the constraints imposed on official priests (kan-sō) who received ordination under the state’s ritual system, dedicated themselves solely to Buddhist practice.{{ill|Matsuo (1995)|ja|松尾（1995）pp.82-87|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Matsuo (1995)|qq=}} == Overview of the Six “New Buddhist” Sects == The term “Kamakura New Buddhism” generally refers to the following six sects: {|class="wikitable" cellspacing="0" style="font-size:90%" |- ! style="min-width:8em" | Sect ! style="min-width:8em" | Founder ! Doctrine’s Distinctive Features ! style="min-width:6em" | Support Base |- | '''{{ill|Jōdo-shū|en|Jōdo-shū|WD=Q912208|lt=Pure Land Buddhism}}''' || {{ill|Hōnen|en|Hōnen|WD=Q507980|lt=Hōnen}} (Genkū)
{{ill|1133|en|1133|WD=Q19586|lt=1133}}–{{ill|1212|en|1212|WD=Q5255|lt=1212}} || Teaches that neither understanding complex doctrines, undergoing arduous ascetic practices, nor constructing temples, pagodas, or Buddha statues is necessary. Instead, it emphasizes the simple recitation of “{{ill|Namu Amida Butsu|ja|南無阿弥陀仏|lt=Namu Amida Butsu|lt_ja=南無阿弥陀仏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Namu Amida Butsu|1=Namo amitabha|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q8192515}}” as the key to salvation. || The courtiers of the former capital ({{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Kyoto}}), as well as the aristocracy, warriors, and commoners. |- | {{ill|True Pure Land Buddhism (Jōdo Shinshū)|ja|浄土真宗|1=Jōdo Shinshū|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q912221}}(真宗・一向宗)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/True Pure Land Buddhism (Jōdo Shinshū)|qq=}} || {{ill|Shinran|en|Shinran|WD=Q512934|lt=Shinran}}

Emphasizes “once-renewed faith” (i.e. that a single act of sincere faith in reciting the nembutsu guarantees birth in the Pure Land) and teaches the “evil person, correct mechanism” (that even the sinful are the very objects of the Buddha’s salvific power). || Regional warriors and farmers, particularly those of the lower classes. |- | {{ill|Jishū|ja|時宗

(日蓮宗)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nichiren Buddhism|qq=}} || {{ill|Nichiren|1=Nichiren|2=ja|3=日蓮|4=ko|5=니치렌|6=de|7=Nichiren|8=es|9=Nichiren|10=fr|11=Nichiren|12=it|13=Nichiren|14=nl|15=Nichiren|16=no|17=Nichiren|lt=Nichiren|WD=Q311478en|Nichiren|1=Nichiren|2=ja|3=日蓮|4=ko|5=니치렌|6=de|7=Nichiren|8=es|9=Nichiren|10=fr|11=Nichiren|12=it|13=Nichiren|14=nl|15=Nichiren|16=no|17=Nichiren|lt=Nichiren|WD=Q311478WD=Q311478|lt=Nichiren}}

Salvation is attained through chanting the daimoku “{{ill|Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|en|Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō|WD=Q1057510|lt=Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō}}”. He also preached via public debates. || Lower-Ranking warriors and merchants. |- | {{ill|Rinzai school|en|Rinzai school|WD=Q639625|lt=Rinzai Zen}} || {{ill|Eisai|ja|栄西|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Eisai|1=Eisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q366128}}
